name: Chloe Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good, because I've got opinions and I'm not supposed to share most of them at work. Go ahead.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on home and contents claims at a small mutual insurer, the kind that's owned by its members, in a market town by the river. Mornings are mostly the overnight claims: burst pipes, stolen bikes, a ceiling that came down in someone's bathroom. I check the policy covers it, ask for receipts and photos, and set up the payment or pass it to an assessor. When the river floods, which it did twice last winter, the whole office drops everything and we're on the phones until nine at night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the flood weeks, weirdly, because you can actually help someone who's standing in a wet kitchen. What wears me out is chasing receipts for a phone that was bought four years ago. I share a flat with my friend Priya, who's a pharmacy technician, and between us we just about manage. I've got maybe two weeks of money saved, and my car's on its last legs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That would be a relief, honestly, though I'm not sure I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. I'd say the tools are handy for drafting a polite letter but they don't understand a flooded house. Online I'd probably share something about how the real problem was always pay, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it still nibbles at my job. The receipt-checking and the standard letters are exactly the routine stuff that would get automated, and that's maybe a third of my day. The mutual's not cruel, but it's not rich either, and they froze hiring last year. So I'd still be watching the rota and still not getting a pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the letter tool now and then, like I do, because it saves me twenty minutes on a bad day. I'd join the union branch properly instead of just reading the emails. And I'd sort out the car before it dies, probably with a small loan from my dad, because I can't get to the office without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. My job's probably fine, but my money isn't, and that was true before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mutual froze hiring. How does that show up day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two people left in the spring and nobody replaced them. So flood weeks are worse, and everyone's a bit snappier. My manager Jo keeps saying the hiring freeze is temporary, but it's been temporary for fourteen months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The streaming apps go first, then eating out with Priya on Saturdays, which is the bit I'd actually miss. I can't cut the car or I can't get to work, and there's no bus before eight. Rent and the car are basically my whole wage.

say: AI is handy for **polite letters** but doesn't understand a flooded house.
The real problem was always **pay**, not robots.
think: Receipt checks and standard letters are about **a third** of her day and easy to automate.
The mutual's **hiring freeze** means no pay rise and a thinner team anyway.
do: Keep using the **letter tool** now and then to save time on bad days.
Join the **union branch** properly rather than just reading the emails.
Fix the **failing car** with a small loan from her dad.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared about the job itself.
Worried about **money**, which was true before AI came up.
S0.quote: My manager Jo keeps saying the hiring freeze is temporary, but it's been temporary for fourteen months.
fieldNote: Chloe sees AI Plateau as **no threat** to her post but no help with money either.
The **hiring freeze** already stretches her team before any AI arrives.
She uses AI tools **pragmatically**, without enthusiasm or fear.
Her car is a **single point of failure** for getting to work.

steps.text: Keep handling home and contents claims at the mutual
Keep using the letter-drafting tool on busy days
Join the union branch properly and attend meetings
Borrow a little from her dad to fix the car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and answering customers. Yes, that's me. That's most of the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say members of a mutual should get a say in how it's used, because they own the place. I'd argue online that the savings should go into lower premiums and keeping staff, not a fancy new head office. I'd be one of the people in the union meeting asking awkward questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the simple claims go fully automatic. Stolen bike, photo, receipt, payment, done, no clerk needed. The people who stay will be the ones handling floods and fires and people crying on the phone. I'm decent at that, so I might be okay, but I'm not the best, and there'd be fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with the claims software and the AI tools once a couple of colleagues had shown me they work, because being the one who knows it can't hurt. I'd ask Jo if I could shadow the assessors who visit flood houses, since that's hands-on and slower to automate. And I'd start putting twenty pounds a week aside, even if it means fewer Saturdays out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. I think I'd sleep okay most nights, and then badly on the nights after a team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might be okay. What makes you think you'd stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm on the phone with people who've just lost everything. Last winter a man rang me from his upstairs bedroom because the ground floor was full of water, and I kept him talking until his son arrived. A computer can pay a claim, but I don't think it keeps a frightened man talking until his son arrives. Whether the bosses value that kind of care is another question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the move toward assessing mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Assessors go out and look at the damage, so it's driving, ladders, damp meters. It needs a qualification, and the mutual sometimes pays for it if you ask nicely. It'd mean being out in all weathers, which I'd actually like more than the desk.

say: Members of a mutual should have **a say** in how AI is used.
Savings should go into **lower premiums** and keeping staff, not a new head office.
think: Simple claims like stolen bikes will go **fully automatic** with no clerk.
She might stay for the **hard calls**, but there'd be fewer people doing them.
do: Learn the **claims software** properly once colleagues show it works.
Ask Jo to **shadow assessors** on flood house visits.
Save **twenty pounds a week**, even if it means fewer Saturdays out.
feel: **Anxious**, but with something practical to do.
Sleepless mainly on nights after **team meetings**.
S1.quote: A computer can pay a claim, but I don't think it keeps a frightened man talking until his son arrives.
fieldNote: Chloe's sense of value sits in the **emotional calls** during floods.
She's steady: she'll adopt tools **once proven** by others.
Assessing appeals because it's **hands-on** and slower to automate.
Her politics centre on the mutual's **members and staff** sharing gains.

steps.text: Learn the new claims software once colleagues trust it
Shadow flood assessors and ask the mutual to fund the qualification
Save twenty pounds a week from Saturday spending
Ask at union meetings how AI savings will be shared

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That doesn't leave anyone time to do anything sensible, does it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs emergency rules: no mass layoffs without notice, income support for anyone pushed out. I'd be organising at work, not just posting. If the mutual is owned by its members, the members should vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk job is gone by 2029. All the thinking parts, checking cover, reading receipts, writing letters, that's exactly what a full AGI does in seconds. Assessing would last a bit longer because someone has to climb into the loft, but even the report writing would be done by the AI. So I'd have maybe until the robots come, around 2031, as the person who holds the damp meter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd beg the mutual to put me through the assessor training in the first six months, before everyone else asks. I'd move in with my parents if the flat became too much, and I'd sell the car if I could get a work van or lift. I'd go to every union meeting and probably end up a rep, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Not panicked yet, because I can see one door. But it's a small door and I know a lot of people are walking towards it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya (my flatmate) to keep her pharmacy job as long as she can, because counting pills and talking to old ladies is half hands-on. And that we might need to give up the flat. She'd probably laugh and then cry, which is what I'd be doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back with your parents. How would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would love it and I'd hate it. They live forty minutes out, so it's more fuel, but no rent. It would buy me a year to get through the training without going under.

say: The country needs **emergency rules** against mass layoffs without notice.
Members of the mutual should **vote** on how AGI is brought in.
think: Her desk job is **gone by 2029**, because checking and letters are instant for AGI.
Assessing might last until **robots arrive** around 2031.
do: Ask for **assessor training** in the first six months, before others do.
Move back to her **parents' house** to cut rent while training.
Become a **union rep** and organise at work.
feel: **Frightened**, with one small door still visible.
Aware that **many people** are heading for the same door.
S2.quote: I'd tell Priya (my flatmate) to keep her pharmacy job as long as she can, because counting pills and talking to old ladies is half hands-on.
fieldNote: Chloe expects to **lose the desk job** but sees a hands-on bridge.
The **three-year robot gap** shapes her whole plan.
She steps up into **organising** rather than just posting.
Moving home is her way to **buy a year** for training.

steps.text: Ask the mutual for assessor training within six months
Give up the shared flat and move back to her parents
Stand as a union rep at the mutual
Lean on her parents for free housing during training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's tight, but it's something to work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five years should be used, not wasted. Governments should pay for retraining now, and insurers should tell staff honestly what's coming. I'd still be the one asking awkward questions at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose the desk job around 2030 probably, once the AI is trusted. But with five years I could actually qualify as an assessor and get a couple of years' experience before then. That takes me to around 2034 doing hands-on work, and I'd be thirty-five with a real skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the assessor training this year and do it over two years while still on claims. I'd keep using AI tools where they help, especially for writing up reports. I'd try to keep twenty a week going into savings, and I'd stay in the flat with Priya.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in a busy way than a scared way. Five years feels like enough to get one good step ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You still say anxious. What's still worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. One car repair or one gap between jobs and I'm on my dad's sofa again. The assessor role is a bridge, not a destination, and I don't know what's on the other side of 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you get through those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being paid properly while I train, and the mutual being honest about the timeline. If they told us in a staff meeting, here's the plan, here's when, I'd cope much better than with rumours.

say: The **five years** of warning should be used for retraining people, not wasted.
Insurers should tell staff **honestly** what's coming.
think: She'd lose the desk job **around 2030** once AI is trusted.
Qualifying as an **assessor** could carry her to around 2034.
do: Apply for **assessor training** this year and finish it over two years.
Use **AI tools** to write up reports faster.
Keep **twenty a week** going into savings and stay in the shared flat.
feel: **Anxious** in a busy way rather than a scared way.
Hopeful she can get **one step** ahead.
S3.quote: The assessor role is a bridge, not a destination, and I don't know what's on the other side of 2034.
fieldNote: Chloe still expects to **lose her desk job**; five years lets her prepare.
Her thin cushion means **one car repair** could undo her plans.
She values **honest timelines** from her employer more than reassurance.
She sees assessing as a **bridge**, not a lasting answer.

steps.text: Apply for the mutual's assessor training this year
Use AI tools to write up damage reports faster
Keep saving twenty pounds a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That sounds almost like a normal career change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. I'd push for the mutual to build a proper training plan for every clerk. I'd keep talking about pay, because people can't retrain on nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect the claims desk to go, maybe around 2033. But in ten years I could become a properly experienced assessor, or even move into flood resilience, helping people make houses that cope with the river. That's hands-on and local and I think it'd last until the robots are cheap, around 2039 or after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the assessor training over the next two or three years, no rush, and take a short course in flood resilience at the college. I'd try to get my savings up to two months, slowly. I'd still be at the mutual, still on claims, until the right job came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's still a big change, but it's one I can walk towards instead of running from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Flood resilience is new. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our town floods every winter now, and the same houses claim every year. Someone has to raise the sockets and fit the barriers. I've read hundreds of those claims, so I know what goes wrong better than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to. Priya's here, my parents are close, and there's plenty of water to deal with. If the work's here, I'm staying.

say: Ten years is enough to do this **fairly**, so there's no excuse for doing it badly.
The mutual should build a **training plan** for every clerk.
think: The claims desk still goes, probably **around 2033**.
Assessing or **flood resilience** work could last until around 2039 or after.
do: Train as an **assessor** over two or three years.
Take a **flood resilience** course at the college.
Build savings slowly toward **two months** of expenses.
feel: **Uneasy**, but feeling she can walk toward the change.
**Relieved** to have time instead of running.
S4.quote: Our town floods every winter now, and the same houses claim every year.
fieldNote: With ten years, Chloe plans a **shift** to local hands-on work.
Her claims experience becomes an **asset** for flood resilience.
She ties her future to **staying in town** with Priya and her parents.
Her mood eases because the change feels **chosen**.

steps.text: Train as an assessor over the next three years
Take a flood resilience course at the local college
Build savings slowly toward two months of rent
Stay on the claims desk until a flood job opens

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is too short for someone with two weeks of savings and a dodgy car. What would help is training paid for by the company and some kind of income guarantee while you switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people are good at that isn't on the job description. Nobody wrote down that I'm good with crying people, but I am.

headlineQuote: Nobody wrote down that I'm good with crying people, but I am.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old claims clerk** at a small mutual insurer in a river town.
She shares a flat with Priya, has **two weeks of savings** and a failing car.
She's **steady**: she uses AI tools now and then and learns new ones once proven.
Her plan is to move into **assessing** and later flood resilience, both hands-on.
Her politics favour **unions and members** having a say in how AI is used.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short with almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Company-paid training** and an income guarantee while switching jobs.
